subject: Nonfarm Payrolls Data Looms
body_text:

 Good morning! Here's the latest in trending: 

 New robotaxi: Tesla ( TSLA ) will offer Cybercab rides in Austin today after a fairly muted launch event.

 Weak results: Lululemon ( LULU ) sinks as it cuts FY guidance  again ahead of new CEO taking over.

 More layoffs: Volkswagen ( VWAGY ) expands restructuring drive with 50,000 additional job cuts .
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Top News
 
 
 
 Employment gauge 
 
 
 
Getty Images
 
 
This year's job growth trend has improved from last year's addition of a measly 15K jobs per month. Don't expect the progress to continue in August's nonfarm payrolls data... as the upcoming report may be driven by one-time factors.

 What to expect: Economists expect nonfarm payrolls to increase by 55K in August, compared to July's 23K decline. "The August report might be more noise than signal," said KPMG Chief Economist Diane Swonk. The loss of temporary protected status  (TPS) for 330K Haitian immigrants tops the list of potential disruptors in August. About 200K had work permits and, with the TPS loss, employers would have to let them go unless they have other work visas. But this won't be reflected in the unemployment and labor force participation rates as the workers no longer belong to the U.S. labor force. Recent meat-processing plant closures could also "muddy the figures," Swonk said. As a result, she thinks the 55K consensus estimate may be optimistic and "there's a real potential that that could be a negative number." 

Historical trends provide another reason to keep expectations low. "August has a long history of the last 10 years of disappointing initially on the downside," Swonk said, as initial response rates tend to be lower. There are a few positive factors that may partly offset the negative ones. The July JOLTS report showed a "steady as she goes" labor market, indicating a "low hire, low fire" environment. A seasonal dynamic in education hiring could also help bolster employment numbers. The unemployment rate is expected to tick up from 4.1% in July to 4.2% in August – but it's still a low level by historical standards. Wage growth is seen cooling in August – "evidence that recent declines in the unemployment rate do not reflect a retightening labor market," said Citi economist Veronica Clark.

 SA commentary:  "By and large, all the data has to do is come in as expected," Investing Group Leader Mott Capital Management said, meaning it should either be unchanged or show minimal improvements from July. "Numbers that come in stronger than expected could easily put even more pressure on the Fed to hike rates ," Mott Capital pointed out. "Numbers that come in weaker than expected would alter everything, put downward pressure on rates, and give the Fed time until November to see what happens." SA analyst Deep Value Investing thinks an important reading today will be the labor force participation rate. "I think the days when payrolls go up and unemployment goes down are behind us," they said. "Another item that I will keep a very close eye on is the revisions to prior payrolls."  Private Hiring Grinds To A Near-Halt
